content:
Matrices look mechanical, so students race through them and drop easy marks. The real traps hide in order compatibility and the fact that AB rarely equals BA. Take the free JEE Matrices online test below. It holds 15 exam-pattern MCQs with instant scoring and worked answers. Aim for 12 out of 15, then fix the ones you miss.

What JEE asks from Matrices

  • Order, equality and the common types of matrices.
  • Addition, scalar multiplication and their basic properties.
  • Matrix multiplication and its non commutative nature.
  • Transpose along with symmetric and skew symmetric forms.
  • Invertible matrices, adjoint and the trace property.

Formulas and facts to revise first

  • Two matrices add only when they share the same order.
  • The product AB exists only when columns of A match rows of B.
  • Trace of AB equals trace of BA, even though AB and BA differ.
  • A matrix has an inverse only when it stays non singular.
  • The zero matrix acts as the additive identity for its order.

Mistakes that cost JEE marks

  • Assuming AB equals BA and cancelling matrices like plain numbers.
  • Multiplying two orders that simply do not line up.
  • Reading AB equals zero as A zero or B zero.
  • Forgetting that a singular matrix has no inverse at all.

quiz.title: JEE Matrices Quiz
quiz.intro: Fifteen exam-pattern questions. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: If A and B are square matrices of the same order, which trace property always holds?
questions.explanation: The trace stays invariant under cyclic order. So Trace(AB) always equals Trace(BA).

questions.q: If A and B are square matrices of order 3 with AB = A and BA = B, then A² + B² equals:
questions.explanation: A² = A(BA) = (AB)A = A, and likewise B² = B. Adding them gives A + B.
Its transpose equals its inverse, so a permutation matrix is orthogonal.

questions.q: If a matrix has 12 elements, which orders can it take?
questions.explanation: Each order is a factor pair of 12. All six pairs are valid.

questions.q: A matrix with only one row and any number of columns is called a:
questions.explanation: A single row of entries defines a row matrix.

questions.q: Which statement defines an identity matrix of order n?
options: A diagonal matrix where all diagonal elements are 0
A scalar matrix with non-zero diagonal elements
A diagonal matrix where all diagonal elements are 1
A square matrix with all elements as 1
questions.explanation: An identity matrix is diagonal with every diagonal entry equal to 1.

questions.q: If two matrices A and B are equal, then they must have:
options: The same number of rows but any number of columns
The same number of columns but any number of rows
Different orders but the same elements
The same order and corresponding elements equal
questions.explanation: Equal matrices share the same order, and every matching entry agrees.

questions.q: A scalar matrix is a diagonal matrix whose principal diagonal elements are all:
questions.explanation: A scalar matrix repeats one constant along the diagonal, so all diagonal entries are equal.

questions.q: Which property holds for matrix addition?
questions.explanation: Matrix addition follows both A + B = B + A and A + (B + C) = (A + B) + C.

questions.q: The additive identity for a matrix A of order m × n is:
options: Zero matrix of order m × n
questions.explanation: Adding the zero matrix of the same order leaves A unchanged.

questions.q: If A has order 3 × 4 and B has order 4 × 5, what is the order of AB?
questions.explanation: The inner sizes match, so the product takes the outer sizes 3 × 5.

questions.q: If A has order 2 × 3 and B has order 3 × 2, then:
options: Both AB and BA have the same order
Both AB and BA are defined but with different orders
questions.explanation: AB is 2 × 2 while BA is 3 × 3, so both exist with different orders.
For most matrices AB differs from BA, so multiplication is not commutative.

questions.q: For matrices A, B and C with compatible orders, the associative law states:
questions.explanation: Grouping does not change a product, so A(BC) equals (AB)C.

questions.q: If A and B satisfy AB = O, the zero matrix, then:
options: A = O or B = O is necessary
Neither A = O nor B = O is necessary
Both A and B must be zero matrices
A must be an identity matrix
questions.explanation: Two non-zero matrices can multiply to the zero matrix, so neither must be zero.
